newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico names lawyer to lead war on drugs.
newsitem.headline: Mexico names lawyer to lead war on drugs.

text.p: Mexico named a little-known lawyer on Monday to head the country's war on drugs, replacing a general who was fired and jailed last month on charges of taking bribes from a cocaine king.

Attorney-General Jorge Madrazo announced at a news conference that Mariano Herran Salvatti would take over the National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD) with a mandate to root out corruption and clean up the organisation.

Herran replaces Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, a distinguished top military officer who was abruptly imprisoned after the government said it found he was in the pay of Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the country's top drug lord.

The Gutierrez scandal caused an uproar in Washington, where members of Congress said it showed how far traffickers had penetrated Mexican government institutions, and deeply embarrassed President Ernesto Zedillo.
Taking no chances, Madrazo said Herran, a longtime lawyer and magistrate, had passed drug, character and lie detector tests, had his wealth checked and his family investigated before being named.
"I am certain that the new commissioner of the National Institute for Drug Combat will do an efficient, loyal and honest job in fulfilling a difficult and complex mission," Madrazo told reporters.

Herran, 48, hails from the southwestern state of Chiapas. He began his career as a lawyer and held posts as chief legal adviser in the Education Ministry and magistrate in the Federal Conciliation and Arbitration Tribunal before becoming a deputy chief federal prosecutor.

Madrazo said Herran would carry out a "deep-seated restructuring" of the INCD, which has been plagued by allegations of corruption since it was created by President Carlos Salinas de Gortari during his 1988-94 administration.
"Mexican society can fully trust that this restructuring will not be a mere change of name or a cosmetic reform," Madrazo said.

"On the contrary, what we are seeking with the help of a working group of 12 legal experts, is a far-reaching change which includes the legal status of the organisation, its composition, organisation, structures, strategies and methods of investigation," he said.
All current and future INCD personnel would be required to pass drug and character tests carried out by external consultants before being confirmed in their jobs, he added.
In return, staff would be better paid and given improved security protection, he said.

Zedillo, under heavy pressure from Washington to show results in the drug war, has declared the fight against the traffickers who smuggle tons of cocaine, marijuana and heroin across the border into the United States each year, to be Mexico's top national security priority.
